To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) humans and machines are equally accurate in the presence of challenging illumination and appearance-based variation in frontal view faces; (2) humans are less accurate than machines in the absence of challenging variation; and (3) humans are less affected by challenging variation than machines.

(1) humans are more accurate than face recognition algorithms when matching images of the same person taken under challenging, uncontrolled lighting conditions; (2) humans and algorithms are comparably accurate under these conditions, suggesting that face recognition algorithms are ready for real-world applications that require matching faces in challenging conditions; and (3) algorithms are more accurate than humans under less challenging conditions, perhaps because humans do not make use of view-specific information in the same way as the algorithms.
